The original methods and indexed task descriptions validate a wearable dyskinesia monitor in 12 Parkinson patients and eight controls. Activities such as eating and drinking are movement-provocation tasks. The index shows separate methods for acceleration and dyskinesia ratings and treats tremor as a signal to distinguish. The work does not compare raw fig consumption or measure a dietary effect on resting tremor.

The indexed original methods and one-year results describe an open-label series of 30 people with advanced Parkinson disease, with blinded ratings of recorded examinations. Motor scores, time off medication benefit, dyskinesia and other outcomes are measured following deep brain stimulation. Tremor at baseline is considered in interpreting motor response. The article does not compare food exposures or attribute a resting-tremor response to raw fig.

The exact publisher index confirms a 15-person postsurgical stimulation series and exposes its opening discussion. The public PDF and indexed repository landing did not supply a sufficient original methods or outcomes section for this review. Obtain the exact issue pages and check how tremor was measured in the stimulation states.

The original participant and testing sections record baseline rest tremor in four of nine Parkinson participants. The experiment compares passive-movement perception with stimulation on and off and in seven controls. Its measured outcome is detection of movement direction, with no raw-fig exposure comparison or resting-tremor response attributed to any food.

The original methods compare responses recorded from wrist muscles in 45 people with Parkinson disease and 23 controls, using a standardized task. The outcome is evoked suppression of muscle activity, rather than an effect of food or measured change in resting tremor. No raw-fig exposure comparison appears in the verified original procedure.
